back: A form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule, O₃.

front: Where is the ozone layer and what does it do?
back: In the stratosphere (about 15–35 km up); it absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV radiation.
Chlorofluorocarbons: unreactive compounds of C, Cl and F once used in fridges, aerosols and foams.
UV releases chlorine atoms from CFCs in the stratosphere; each Cl atom breaks down ozone and is regenerated.
Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂; ClO + O → Cl + O₂ (overall O₃ + O → 2O₂).
More UV: skin cancer, cataracts, sunburn, weaker immunity, damage to crops and plankton.

front: When was the Montreal Protocol agreed, and what did it do?
back: 1987: it phased out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances.
Halons (fire extinguishers) and methyl bromide (soil fumigant).
Hydrocarbons (e.g. isobutane) and HFCs, which contain no chlorine.
No: high up it protects us from UV; at ground level it is a harmful pollutant in smog.
